title: Pharmacists Urge GLP-1 Users to Rethink Diet as Side Effects Mount
excerpt: With 11% of American adults now on weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy, pharmacists and dietitians say what patients eat matters far more than how much — and the wrong choices can make gastrointestinal side effects significantly worse.
body:
• Kroger Health has launched a GLP-1 Complete Support program pairing pharmacists with registered dietitians to help patients navigate nutrition, side effects, and affordability.
  • Experts recommend 25 to 30 grams of protein per meal and at least 25 grams of fiber daily to counteract muscle loss and constipation, two of the most common issues on GLP-1 drugs.
  • A Gallup survey found 11% of U.S. adults are currently taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss, nearly four times the 3% reported in 2024.
  • New research in the Journal of Nutrition suggests fiber supplementation can improve bowel function and stool consistency for patients experiencing gastrointestinal side effects from GLP-1 drugs.

As GLP-1 weight-loss medications become a mainstream fixture of American healthcare, pharmacists are stepping beyond the dispensing counter to address a growing blind spot: what patients actually eat while on the drugs.

Kroger Health this week unveiled its GLP-1 Complete Support program, connecting patients with pharmacists, registered dietitians, and clinical services to manage the nutritional demands that come with medications like semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound). The program also helps patients navigate affordability through options like the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program.

"Patients need more than a prescription — they need ongoing support. GLP-1 Complete Support was created to help patients navigate affordability, nutrition, and lifestyle changes with confidence."

— Colleen Lindholz, President of Kroger Health

The Scale of the Problem

The urgency behind such programs is clear from the numbers. A Gallup survey of more than 5,000 adults, conducted between late May and early June 2026, found that 11% of Americans ages 18 and older are currently taking GLP-1 drugs for weight loss — nearly four times the 3% who reported doing so in 2024. Fifteen percent said they had used the medications at some point.

That surge has coincided with a dip in the national obesity rate, which fell from a record 39.9% in 2022 to 36.4% in 2026. But as prescriptions multiply, so do reports of side effects. The most common complaints are gastrointestinal — nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation — and diet plays a central role in how severe they become.

Protein First, Then Fiber

The emerging consensus among clinicians is straightforward: because GLP-1 drugs suppress appetite, every calorie patients do consume carries more weight. Kroger Health dietitians advise building meals around protein — seafood, lean meats, eggs, Greek yogurt, beans, or tofu — before adding fruits, vegetables, and whole grains.

Caroline Messer, an endocrinologist at Northwell Lenox Hill Hospital in New York, recommends 25 to 30 grams of protein per meal for both men and women on these medications. Rapid weight loss often strips muscle along with fat, and adequate protein intake combined with strength training is the primary defense against that.

Fiber is the other pillar. An expert consensus statement published in the journal Obesity recommends at least 25 grams of daily fiber for women and 30 grams for men during GLP-1 treatment. High-fiber foods — chia seeds, green peas, quinoa, raspberries, black beans — help manage constipation, one of the drugs' most persistent side effects. A research review published in the Journal of Nutrition found that fiber supplementation improved bowel function and stool consistency in patients experiencing gastrointestinal distress from GLP-1 receptor agonists.

"GLP-1 medications can be powerful tools, but long-term success depends on the everyday choices patients make around food, hydration, and lifestyle."

— Laura Brown, MS, RDN, LDN, Director of Nutrition, Kroger Health

Hydration and Meal Timing

Pharmacists and dietitians also stress hydration. Many patients unintentionally drink less while on GLP-1 drugs, either because their overall appetite drops or because nausea makes them avoid liquids. That can trigger fatigue, dizziness, and worsen constipation.

Priya Jaisinghani, an endocrinologist at NYU Langone Health, advises patients to eat smaller, more frequent meals rather than two or three large ones. Because GLP-1 medications slow gastric emptying, large portions can lead to painful bloating and reflux. She also recommends leaving several hours between dinner and bedtime to reduce acid reflux risk.

For patients just starting the drugs or increasing their dose, soft and blended foods — Greek yogurt, overnight oats, smoothies, protein shakes — are often better tolerated. Tara Schmidt, lead dietitian for the Mayo Clinic Diet, notes that these options still deliver protein, fiber, and hydration while putting less stress on the digestive system.

What New Research Shows

A growing body of academic work is formalizing these recommendations. A narrative review published in Advances in Nutrition in June 2026 examined how dietary fiber and GLP-1 drugs interact, finding that fibers can mitigate drug-related constipation, stabilize the gut microbiota, and potentially extend the metabolic benefits of treatment even after patients stop taking the medication.

Separately, a UK study by MMR Research of 974 adults found that 77% of GLP-1 users said the drugs changed how they experience food. Nearly a third reported altered taste perception, with 30% going off fatty foods and 29% finding sugary items intolerable. Almost half said sweet flavors felt far more intense than before.

What's Next

The Kroger program is part of a broader shift in how pharmacies engage with GLP-1 patients. As oral versions of these drugs — including a daily Wegovy pill approved in December 2025 and Eli Lilly's Foundayo approved in April 2026 — make the medications accessible to even more people, the demand for structured nutritional support is expected to grow.

For the millions of Americans already on these drugs, the message from pharmacists is consistent: a prescription alone is not a plan. The foods patients choose, the water they drink, and the habits they build around meals will determine whether the weight they lose stays off — and whether the side effects remain manageable.
